# Book I, Proposition 9

*Bisecting an angle*

> To bisect a given rectilineal angle.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/09-idea.svg" alt="Mark equal lengths on the two arms (blue) and build an equilateral triangle on the gap (yellow): the line from the corner to its tip splits the angle into equal halves (red)." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>Mark equal lengths on the two arms (blue) and build an equilateral triangle on the gap (yellow): the line from the corner to its tip splits the angle into equal halves (red).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/09.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.9, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let the angle BAC be the given rectilineal angle.

It is then required to bisect it.

Let a point D be taken at random on AB;

let AE be cut off from AC equal to AD; [I. 3]

let DE be joined, and on DE let the equilateral triangle DEF be constructed;

let AF be joined.

I say that the angle BAC has been bisected by the straight line AF.

For, since AD is equal to AE,

and AF is common,

the two sides DA, AF are equal to the two sides EA, AF respectively.

And the base DF is equal to the base EF;

therefore the angle DAF is equal to the angle EAF. [I. 8]

Therefore the given rectilineal angle BAC has been bisected by the straight line AF.

Q. E. F.

```lean
/-! ## What Euclid reads off the figure -/

/-- Euclid's chance point `D` on `AB`. He takes it at random, but in the next breath
cuts off from `AC` a straight line equal to `AD` [I. 3], so `AD` must be less than
`AC`. A circle about `A` through `C` keeps `D` in: `D` is taken between `A` and `B`
if `B` is not outside that circle, or between `A` and the point where `AB` leaves
it if `B` is outside. -/
theorem Prop9.chance_point {A B C : Point} (hAB : A ≠ B) (hAC : A ≠ C) :
    ∃ D : Point, Between A D B ∧ ‖A D‖ < ‖A C‖ := by
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
  obtain ⟨α, hA_α, hC_α⟩ := Postulate3 A C hAC
  have hA_in : InsideCircle A α ∨ OnCircle A α := Or.inl (centre_inside hA_α)
  by_cases hB_α : InsideCircle B α ∨ OnCircle B α
  · /- `B` is not outside the circle: any point between `A` and `B` is inside it
       (System E, Circle 2). -/
    obtain ⟨D, -, hADB, -⟩ := exists_point_between hA_AB hB_AB hAB []
    exact ⟨D, hADB, len_lt_of_inside hA_α hC_α (inside_of_between hA_in hB_α hADB)⟩
  · /- `B` is outside: `AB` leaves the circle at a point `X` between `A` and `B`
       (Intersections 4), and `D` is taken between `A` and `X`. -/
    have hB_out : OutsideCircle B α := ⟨fun h => hB_α (Or.inl h), fun h => hB_α (Or.inr h)⟩
    obtain ⟨X, hX_α, hX_AB, hAXB⟩ := line_circle_between (centre_inside hA_α) hA_AB hB_out hB_AB
    obtain ⟨D, -, hADX, -⟩ := exists_point_between hA_AB hX_AB (ne_of_between hAXB) []
    exact ⟨D, between_of_between_left hAXB hADX,
      len_lt_of_inside hA_α hC_α (inside_of_between hA_in (Or.inr hX_α) hADX)⟩

/-- A point on `Q`'s side of the straight line `AB`, where `Q` is on the other side
from `R`, is itself on the other side from `R`: a straight line has only two sides. -/
theorem Prop9.opposite {P Q R A B : Point} (hPQ : SameSideOf P Q A B)
    (hQR : OppositeSidesOf Q R A B) : OppositeSidesOf P R A B := by
  refine ⟨hPQ.1, fun L hA hB => ?_⟩
  have hs : SameSide P Q L := hPQ.2 L hA hB
  have ho : OppositeSides Q R L := hQR.2 L hA hB
  exact ⟨not_on_line_of_same_side hs, ho.2.1, fun h => ho.2.2 (same_side_trans hs h)⟩

/-- Proclus' objector, first case: `F` might fall on `AB` itself, beyond `D`. Proclus
answers him with the second part of I.5 (Heath, vol. 1, p. 265). Since `FD` is equal
to `FE`, the angle `FDE` is equal to the angle `FED` [I. 5]. Since `AD` is equal to
`AE`, the angles `EDF`, `DEC` under the base of the triangle `ADE` are equal [I. 5].
So the angle `DEF` is equal to the angle `DEC`, with `F` and `C` on the same side of
`DE`; then `F` lies on the straight line `EC` (`onRay_of_angle_eq`), that is, on `AC`.
But `AB` and `AC` meet only at `A`. -/
theorem Prop9.not_on_arm {A B C D E F : Point} (hBAC : Triangle B A C) (hADB : Between A D B)
    (hAEC : Between A E C) (hAD_AE : ‖A D‖ = ‖A E‖) (hFD_FE : ‖F D‖ = ‖F E‖)
    (hF : OppositeSidesOf F A D E) : ¬ Between A D F := by
  intro hADF
  have hDE : D ≠ E := hF.1
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hBAC.ne₁₂.symm
  obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C hBAC.ne₂₃
  obtain ⟨DE, hD_DE, hE_DE⟩ := Postulate1 D E hDE
  have hFA : OppositeSides F A DE := hF.2 DE hD_DE hE_DE
  have hD_AB : OnLine D AB := on_line_of_between_ends hADB hA_AB hB_AB
  have hE_AC : OnLine E AC := on_line_of_between_ends hAEC hA_AC hC_AC
  have hADE : Triangle A D E := hF.symm.triangle.cab
  have hFDE : Triangle F D E := hF.triangle.cab
  have hFD : F ≠ D := hFDE.ne₁₂
  have hFE : F ≠ E := hFDE.ne₁₃
  /- Since `FD` is equal to `FE`, the angle `FDE` is equal to the angle `FED`. [I. 5] -/
  obtain ⟨G, hFEG⟩ := produce hFE
  have hbase : ∠ F D E = ∠ F E D := (Prop5 hFDE hFD_FE (between_symm hADF) hFEG).1
  /- Since `AD` is equal to `AE`, and `AD`, `AE` are produced to `F`, `C`, the angles
     `EDF`, `DEC` under the base are equal. [I. 5] -/
  have hunder : ∠ E D F = ∠ D E C := (Prop5 hADE hAD_AE hADF hAEC).2
  have hDEC_DEF : ∠ D E C = ∠ D E F :=
    hunder.symm.trans ((angle_symm hDE.symm hFD).trans (hbase.trans (angle_symm hFE hDE)))
  /- `C`, beyond `E` from `A`, is on the other side of `DE` from `A` (Pasch 3), as `F` is;
     so `C` and `F` are on the same side of `DE`. -/
  have hCE : C ≠ E := ne_of_between (between_symm hAEC)
  have hC_DE : ¬ OnLine C DE := fun hC =>
    hFA.2.1 ((line_unique hCE hC hE_DE hC_AC hE_AC) ▸ hA_AC)
  have hCF : SameSide C F DE := by
    rcases same_side_or hFA.2.1 hC_DE hFA.1 (pasch3 hAEC hE_DE) with h | h
    · exact absurd (same_side_symm h) hFA.2.2
    · exact h
  have hray : OnRay C E F :=
    onRay_of_angle_eq (SameSideOf.of_line hDE.symm hE_DE hD_DE hCF) hDEC_DEF
  /- So `F` is on `AC`, and on `AB`; and these meet only at `A`. -/
  have hF_AC : OnLine F AC := hray.symm.onLine hE_AC hC_AC
  have hF_AB : OnLine F AB := on_line_of_between hADF hA_AB hD_AB
  have hAB_AC : AB = AC := line_unique (ne_of_between_ends hADF) hA_AB hF_AB hA_AC hF_AC
  exact hBAC.off_line hB_AB hA_AB (hAB_AC ▸ hC_AC)

/-- Where the straight line `AF` crosses `DE`. Since `F` is on the other side of `DE`
from `A`, the straight line `AF` crosses `DE` at a point `M` (Intersection 1, Pasch
4). And `M` falls between `D` and `E`. It is not `D` or `E`: that is Proclus' first
case, `Prop9.not_on_arm`. Nor is it beyond `D` or beyond `E`: then `D` and `E` would
be on the same side of `AF`, and I.7 would make them one point, since `AD` is equal
to `AE` and `FD` to `FE`. -/
theorem Prop9.crossing {A B C D E F : Point} (hBAC : Triangle B A C) (hADB : Between A D B)
    (hAEC : Between A E C) (hAD_AE : ‖A D‖ = ‖A E‖) (hFD_FE : ‖F D‖ = ‖F E‖)
    (hF : OppositeSidesOf F A D E) : ∃ M : Point, Between A M F ∧ Between D M E := by
  have hDE : D ≠ E := hF.1
  obtain ⟨L, hD_L, hE_L⟩ := Postulate1 D E hDE
  have hFA : OppositeSides F A L := hF.2 L hD_L hE_L
  have hAF : A ≠ F := by
    intro h
    subst h
    exact hFA.2.2 (same_side_refl hFA.2.1)
  obtain ⟨N, hA_N, hF_N⟩ := Postulate1 A F hAF
  obtain ⟨hLN, M, hM_L, hM_N⟩ := lines_meet_of_opposite_sides hFA hF_N hA_N
  have hMA : M ≠ A := fun h => hFA.2.1 (h ▸ hM_L)
  have hMF : M ≠ F := fun h => hFA.1 (h ▸ hM_L)
  have hAMF : Between A M F :=
    pasch4 hLN hM_L hM_N hA_N hF_N hAF hMA.symm hMF.symm (fun h => hFA.2.2 (same_side_symm h))
  refine ⟨M, hAMF, ?_⟩
  /- `M` is not `D`, nor `E`: Proclus' first case, on either arm. -/
  have hDM : D ≠ M := by
    intro h
    rw [← h] at hAMF
    exact Prop9.not_on_arm hBAC hADB hAEC hAD_AE hFD_FE hF hAMF
  have hME : M ≠ E := by
    intro h
    rw [h] at hAMF
    exact Prop9.not_on_arm hBAC.cba hAEC hADB hAD_AE.symm hFD_FE.symm hF.swap hAMF
  /- `D` and `E` are not on the same side of `AF`, or I.7 would make them one point. -/
  have hD_N : ¬ OnLine D N := fun hD => hLN (line_unique hDM hD_L hM_L hD hM_N)
  have hE_N : ¬ OnLine E N := fun hE => hLN (line_unique hME.symm hE_L hM_L hE hM_N)
  have hI7 : ¬ SameSide D E N := fun hs =>
    hDE (Prop7 (SameSideOf.of_line hAF hA_N hF_N hs)
      (by rw [len_symm D A, hAD_AE, len_symm A E]) (by rw [len_symm D F, hFD_FE, len_symm F E]))
  rcases between_cases hDM hME hDE hD_L hM_L hE_L with h | h | h
  · exact h
  · exact absurd (pasch2 h hM_N hD_N) hI7
  · exact absurd (same_side_symm (pasch2 (between_symm h) hM_N hE_N)) hI7

/-- From where `AF` crosses `DE`, the sides of `AB`: `M`, between `D` and `E`, is on
`E`'s side of `AB`, and `F`, beyond `M` from `A`, is on `M`'s side; and `E`, between
`A` and `C`, is on `C`'s side (Pasch 2). So `F` is on `C`'s side of `AB`. -/
theorem Prop9.side {A B C D E F M : Point} (hBAC : Triangle B A C) (hADB : Between A D B)
    (hAEC : Between A E C) (hDME : Between D M E) (hAMF : Between A M F) :
    SameSideOf F C A B := by
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hBAC.ne₁₂.symm
  have hD_AB : OnLine D AB := on_line_of_between_ends hADB hA_AB hB_AB
  have hC_AB : ¬ OnLine C AB := hBAC.off_line hB_AB hA_AB
  have hE_AB : ¬ OnLine E AB := fun h => hC_AB (on_line_of_between hAEC hA_AB h)
  have hM_AB : ¬ OnLine M AB := fun h => hE_AB (on_line_of_between hDME hD_AB h)
  have hME : SameSide M E AB := pasch2 hDME hD_AB hM_AB
  have hMF : SameSide M F AB := pasch2 hAMF hA_AB hM_AB
  have hEC : SameSide E C AB := pasch2 hAEC hA_AB hE_AB
  exact SameSideOf.of_line hBAC.ne₁₂.symm hA_AB hB_AB
    (same_side_trans (same_side_trans hME hMF) hEC)

/-- To bisect a given rectilineal angle. -/
theorem Prop9 {A B C : Point} (hBAC : Triangle B A C) :
    ∃ F : Point, SameSideOf F C A B ∧ SameSideOf F B A C ∧
      ∠ B A F = ∠ F A C ∧ ∠ B A F + ∠ F A C = ∠ B A C := by
  -- Let the angle BAC be the given rectilineal angle.
  have hAB : A ≠ B := hBAC.ne₁₂.symm
  have hAC : A ≠ C := hBAC.ne₂₃
  obtain ⟨AB, hA_AB, hB_AB⟩ := Postulate1 A B hAB
  obtain ⟨AC, hA_AC, hC_AC⟩ := Postulate1 A C hAC
  have hC_AB : ¬ OnLine C AB := hBAC.off_line hB_AB hA_AB
  -- It is then required to bisect it.
  -- Let a point D be taken at random on AB;
  /- At random, but not too far out, since AD is about to be cut off from AC: see
     `Prop9.chance_point`. -/
  obtain ⟨D, hADB, hAD_AC⟩ := Prop9.chance_point hAB hAC
  have hAD : A ≠ D := ne_of_between hADB
  have hD_AB : OnLine D AB := on_line_of_between_ends hADB hA_AB hB_AB
  -- let AE be cut off from AC equal to AD; [I. 3]
  obtain ⟨E, hAEC, hAE_AD⟩ := Prop3 hAD hAD_AC
  have hAE : A ≠ E := ne_of_between hAEC
  have hE_AC : OnLine E AC := on_line_of_between_ends hAEC hA_AC hC_AC
  -- let DE be joined, and on DE let the equilateral triangle DEF be constructed;
  /- E is off AB, or C would be on it; so ADE is a triangle. The equilateral triangle
     goes on the side of DE away from A, which Euclid leaves to his figure: we take a
     point Q on that side (System E, Points 6) and ask I.1 for Q's side. -/
  have hE_AB : ¬ OnLine E AB := fun h => hC_AB (on_line_of_between hAEC hA_AB h)
  have hADE : Triangle A D E := Triangle.of_line hA_AB hD_AB hAD hE_AB
  have hDE : D ≠ E := hADE.ne₂₃
  obtain ⟨Q, hQA, -⟩ := exists_oppositeSidesOf hADE.bca []
  obtain ⟨F, ⟨-, -, hEF_FD⟩, hside⟩ := Prop1 D E hDE Q
  have hFA : OppositeSidesOf F A D E := Prop9.opposite (hside hQA.triangle) hQA
  -- let AF be joined.
  /- Joined, AF falls within the angle BAC. That is Proclus' objector answered: AF
     crosses DE between D and E (`Prop9.crossing`, by I.5 and I.7), and from there F is
     on C's side of AB and on B's side of AC (`Prop9.side`). -/
  have hFD_FE : ‖F D‖ = ‖F E‖ := hEF_FD.symm.trans (len_symm E F)
  obtain ⟨M, hAMF, hDME⟩ := Prop9.crossing hBAC hADB hAEC hAE_AD.symm hFD_FE hFA
  have hFC : SameSideOf F C A B := Prop9.side hBAC hADB hAEC hDME hAMF
  have hFB : SameSideOf F B A C := Prop9.side hBAC.cba hAEC hADB (between_symm hDME) hAMF
  have hF_AB : ¬ OnLine F AB := hFC.triangle.off_line hA_AB hB_AB
  have hF_AC : ¬ OnLine F AC := hFB.triangle.off_line hA_AC hC_AC
  have hAF : A ≠ F := fun h => hF_AB (h ▸ hA_AB)
  -- I say that the angle BAC has been bisected by the straight line AF.
  -- For, since AD is equal to AE,
  have hAD_AE : ‖A D‖ = ‖A E‖ := hAE_AD.symm
  -- and AF is common,
  have hAF_AF : ‖A F‖ = ‖A F‖ := rfl
  -- the two sides DA, AF are equal to the two sides EA, AF respectively.
  -- And the base DF is equal to the base EF;
  have hDF_EF : ‖D F‖ = ‖E F‖ := (len_symm D F).trans hEF_FD.symm
  -- therefore the angle DAF is equal to the angle EAF. [I. 8]
  /- ADF and AEF are triangles, since F is off AB and off AC. -/
  have hADF : Triangle A D F := Triangle.of_line hA_AB hD_AB hAD hF_AB
  have hAEF : Triangle A E F := Triangle.of_line hA_AC hE_AC hAE hF_AC
  have hDAF_EAF : ∠ D A F = ∠ E A F := Prop8 hADF hAEF hAD_AE hAF_AF hDF_EF
  -- Therefore the given rectilineal angle BAC has been bisected by the straight line AF.
  /- The angle DAF is the angle BAF, since D lies on AB, and the angle EAF is the angle
     CAF, that is, FAC, since E lies on AC (an angle depends only on its rays). And
     since F lies within the angle BAC, that angle is made up of BAF and FAC
     (System E, Diagram-angle 2). -/
  have hbisect : ∠ B A F = ∠ F A C := by
    rw [← angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between hADB) hAF.symm, hDAF_EAF,
      angle_onRay_left (OnRay.of_between hAEC) hAF.symm, angle_symm hAC.symm hAF.symm]
  have hAB_AC : AB ≠ AC := fun h => hC_AB (h ▸ hC_AC)
  have hwhole : ∠ B A C = ∠ B A F + ∠ F A C :=
    angle_add_of_inside hA_AB hA_AC hB_AB hC_AC hAB hAC hF_AB hF_AC hAB_AC
      (same_side_symm (hFB.2 AC hA_AC hC_AC)) (same_side_symm (hFC.2 AB hA_AB hB_AB))
  exact ⟨F, hFC, hFB, hbisect, hwhole.symm⟩
  -- Q. E. F.
```

**Reading the figure**

- [`between_cases`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L70): Of three different points on a straight line, one is between the other two. (Between 6)
- [`between_of_between_left`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L63): (Between 4)
- [`between_of_between_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L66): (Between 5)
- [`between_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L41): If `B` is between `A` and `C`, it is between `C` and `A`. (Between 1)
- [`centre_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L33): The centre of a circle is inside it. (Generalities 3)
- [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L178): If each circle passes through a point inside the other, the circles cut one another. This is the step Euclid takes for granted in I.1. (Intersection 5)
- [`circles_meet_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L81): Two circles that cut one another do so on each side of the straight line through their centres. (Intersections 8)
- [`exists_point`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L26): Let a point be taken. (Points 1)
- [`exists_point_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L38): Let a point be taken between `B` and `C`. (Points 3)
- [`exists_point_opposite_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L46): Let a point be taken on the other side of `L` from `B`. (Points 6)
- [`inside_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L140): A circle is "convex": between two points on or inside it, every point is inside. (Circle 2)
- [`line_circle_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L69): A straight line through a point `B` inside a circle, heading out to a point `C` outside it, cuts the circle between `B` and `C`. (Intersections 4)
- [`line_circle_beyond`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L75): A straight line through a point `B` inside a circle, produced beyond `B` away from `C`, cuts the circle there. (Intersections 5)
- [`line_unique`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L26): Two points determine a straight line. (Generalities 1)
- [`lines_meet_of_opposite_sides`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L158): A straight line joining points on opposite sides of `L` crosses `L`. (Intersection 1)
- [`ne_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L44): A point between two others differs from the first. (Between 1)
- [`ne_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L47): The ends of a finite straight line differ. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L50): If `B` is between `A` and `C`, then `A` is not between `B` and `C`. (Between 1)

- [`angle_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L26): The angle `ABC` is the angle `CBA`. (Metric 4)
- [`area_congruent`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L43): Triangles equal in all their sides and angles are equal in area. Euclid uses this without comment once he has shown two triangles congruent. (Metric 9)
- [`area_rotate`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L35): The triangle `ABC` is the triangle `CAB`. (Metric 8)
- [`area_swap`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L38): The triangle `ABC` is the triangle `ACB`. (Metric 8)
- [`eq_of_len_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L17): A finite straight line with distinct ends has length. (Metric 1)
- [`inside_of_len_lt`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L33): A point nearer the centre than the circumference is inside. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L21): If `B` is between `A` and `C`, then `AB` and `BC` together make up `AC`. (Diagram-segment 1)
- [`len_lt_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L37): A point inside is nearer the centre than the circumference. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_self`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L20): The "line" from a point to itself has no length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L23): The line `AB` is the line `BA`. (Metric 3)
- [`same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L49): If the angle `BAC` is nothing, `C` lies on the ray from `A` through `B`. (Diagram-angle 1)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L29): **Superposition.** The triangle `ABC` can be applied to the straight line `L` with `A` on `D`, `B` on the ray from `D` through `G`, and `C` on the side of `L` where `H` is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L25): Adding is commutative. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L44): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L28): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L31): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L34): "Less than" is transitive. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L38): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L41): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

</details>

## Mishnah

**Which side of DE?** Heath: "It will be observed from the translation of this proposition that Euclid does not say, in his description of the construction, that the equilateral triangle should be constructed on the side of DE opposite to A; he leaves this to be inferred from his figure" (vol. 1, p. 264). On A's side, the corner of the triangle can land on A itself, or behind A, and then AF is no straight line at all, or points away from the angle. Proclus worked through those cases for a reader who might claim not to see any room below DE, and Heath finds "no particular value in Proclus' explanation as to how we should proceed in case any one should assert that he could not recognise the existence of any space below DE" (vol. 1, p. 264). Lean infers nothing from a figure, so the side has to be asked for. Book Zero's `exists_oppositeSidesOf` (System E, Points 6) gives a point Q on the far side of DE from A, I.1 as stated here builds the triangle on Q's side, and [`Prop9.opposite`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop09.lean) notes that F is then on the far side from A, since a straight line has only two sides.

**A chance point, again.** As in I.5, D is taken "at random", and in the very next breath AE is cut off from AC equal to AD [I. 3], which needs AD to be the less. So D must not lie too far out along AB. [`Prop9.chance_point`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop09.lean) keeps it inside a circle about A through C: anywhere between A and B if B is not outside that circle, or else between A and the point where AB leaves it (System E, Circle 2 and Intersections 4). It is a circle Euclid never draws.

**Does F fall within the angle?** Heath: "Proclus also answers the possible objection that might be raised to Euclid's proof on the ground that it assumes that, if the equilateral triangle be described on the side of DE opposite to A, its vertex F will lie within the angle BAC. The objector is supposed to argue that this is not necessary, but that F might fall either on one of the lines forming the angle or outside it altogether" (vol. 1, p. 265). In Lean we are that objector, twice over. I.8 wants ADF and AEF to be triangles, so F must be off AB and off AC; and "bisected by the straight line AF", as our statement reads it, says that AF falls within the angle, which I.10 will need. [`Prop9.crossing`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop09.lean) finds the point M where AF crosses the straight line DE (Intersection 1 and Pasch 4) and shows that it lies between D and E. If M were D itself, F would lie on AB, and here the Lean follows Proclus with the second part of I.5: the angles under the base of the isosceles triangle ADE are equal, and so are the angles at the base of DEF, so the angle DEF would be equal to the angle DEC, and F would lie on AC as well as AB (`Prop9.not_on_arm`, with Book Zero's `onRay_of_angle_eq`). Heath: "Here then is the second case in which, in Proclus' view, the second part of I. 5 is useful for refuting objections" (vol. 1, p. 265). If M fell beyond D or beyond E, F would lie outside the angle. Proclus answers that case with I.5 again; the Lean takes the road I.8 has just travelled instead: D and E would be on the same side of AF, each as far from A and from F as the other, and I.7 makes them one point. From M, `Prop9.side` then reads off the sides of AB and AC with Pasch 2.

**What else Lean made us say.** Euclid's conclusion is about the angles DAF and EAF; the angle he set out to bisect is BAC. The angle DAF is the angle BAF because D lies on the ray from A through B, and EAF is FAC because E lies on AC and an angle may be read either way round (`angle_onRay_left` and `angle_symm`, System E's Diagram-angle 4 and Metric 4). That the whole angle BAC is made up of BAF and FAC needs F within it once more (`angle_add_of_inside`, Diagram-angle 2). So the certificate cites I.1, I.5 and I.7 as well as the I.3 and I.8 that Euclid brackets, and it lists Postulate 2, because our I.5 is stated with its sides produced. Every rule cited is one of Jeremy Avigad, Edward Dean and John Mumma's; LeanEuclid, by Logan Murphy, Kaiyu Yang, Jialiang Sun, Zhaoyu Li, Anima Anandkumar and Xujie Si, was open alongside the whole time; and Michael Beeson, Julien Narboux and Freek Wiedijk's *Proof-checking Euclid* is a generous guide to the facts of position that hide in figures like this one.

**Only rectilineal angles.** Proclus, Heath says, takes the chance to insist that the angle be rectilineal, since bisecting curved angles is no matter for an elementary treatise and may not even be possible: "Thus it is difficult to say whether it is possible to bisect the so-called horn-like angle" (vol. 1, p. 265), the angle between a circle and a straight line touching it. Here, too, Proclus gives "his valuable historical note about the trisection of any acute angle, which (as well as the division of an angle in any given ratio) requires resort to other curves than circles" (vol. 1, p. 265): the conchoid of Nicomedes, the quadratrix of Hippias, the spiral of Archimedes. In 1837 Pierre Wantzel proved that straight lines and circles alone cannot trisect every angle: for an angle in general, halving and halving again is all that Euclid's tools can do.

**The modern way.** Put A at the origin, with unit vectors u and v along AB and AC: then u + v, the diagonal of the rhombus on u and v, points along the bisector, just as the diagonal AF of Euclid's kite ADFE does. With complex numbers, arms along e^{iβ} and e^{iγ} have their bisector along e^{i(β+γ)/2}.
